summary: In Greek mythology, Alastor is a Lycian warrior in Sarpedon's host whom Odysseus slays in Iliad 5. Homer later calls Tros "Alastorides," probably marking that Trojan as this Alastor's son. He is distinct from the Pylian Alastor under Nestor, from the Achaean bearer of the wounded, and from Alastor the Neleid.
etymology: Ancient Greek Ἀλάστωρ, "avenging spirit"; also an epithet of Zeus and a name for a vengeful daemon.

sections.heading: Lycian companion of Sarpedon
paragraphs: In Iliad 5 Odysseus, turned by Athena toward the Lycian press, smites Alastor among Chromius, Alcandrus, Halius, Noemon, and Prytanis before Hector intervenes. Ovid recalls the same Lycian death in Metamorphoses 13.

Homer's patronymic Alastorides for Tros (Iliad 10) is usually read as making Tros son of this Lycian Alastor — a link the atlas treats carefully beside the separate node alastor-trojan where that fatherhood is staged.

sections.heading: Homonym care
paragraphs: The atlas id alastor-lycian is the Sarpedonian Lycian alone. Distinct from alastor-pylian (Nestor's array), alastor-achaean (Mecisteus' comrade bearing the wounded), the Neleid Alastor slain by Heracles, and Alastor as epithet or daemon.
